entries.title: The Shape of the First Beloved
entries.summary: From the seven animals and six woven Weights, [[Lyd, The First Beloved]] was born as a single small body—a chimera not in the monstrous sense but in the sense of a synthesis, a living argument that combination was the path to perfection.
entries.body:
From the seven animals and six woven Weights, [[Lyd, The First Beloved]] was born as a single small body—a chimera not in the monstrous sense but in the sense of a synthesis, a living argument that combination was the path to perfection.

In its original form, [[Lyd, The First Beloved]] was small enough to curl in a lap and warm enough to feel like a hearthstone. Its body carried the deep chest and strong hindquarters of the horse, the structural core that gave it solidity beyond its size. Its face was wolf-muzzle and deer-soft eyes, the muzzle sharp and forward-pointing, the eyes holding the amber of sunset and the gold of dawn simultaneously—the [[Auric Aria]]'s own [[Fundamental Frequency]] reflected back from within living flesh. The small velvet antler-buds rose from its crown, warm to the touch, soft as new growth. Its fur shimmered with colors that did not exist in individual animals—moonlit silver at the roots deepening to warm amber at the tips, shifting as it moved the way water shifts in different light, patchlessly perfect in a way no single animal achieves. Its cat's forepaws were delicate and expressive, kneading when it was content, retracting when it was still, the most communicative part of a body that communicated entirely through presence and warmth. Its lark-throat was always ready to sing, a bright little pulse of sound that marked it as alive in the most intimate way. The rabbit's tail was a small impossible cloud of white softness at the base of the spine, perfect and soft and warm, the detail that made it most undeniably beloved rather than simply beautiful.

Its movement was liquid in ways no single animal could achieve—the wolf's directness, the cat's silence, the horse's unhurried weight, the lark's bright motion—all occurring in the same body at the same time without contradiction.

She loved it more than any of her other creations.

Because [[Lyd, The First Beloved]] was not just a creature. It was proof that synthesis worked. It was proof that she could weave disparate things into something that was not just the sum of its parts but more—a new kind of beauty that only existed in the combination.

She named it [[Lyd, The First Beloved]].

It was the First Beloved.

And then it learned to hunt.

### The Hunger

The flaw in the weave did not begin as decay. It began as tracking. A thing made without [[Echoing Bonds]] cannot release what it was made to keep. A thing made without [[Strand]] nor change does not simply wait. It follows the scent of what might restore the missing principle. It hunts the shape of its own absence.

That is why [[Lyd, The First Beloved]] became aggressive.

The first scent it ever learned to hate was blood, not because blood itself was food, but because blood carried the possibility of severance, of injury, of loss, of ending—the fox-shaped interruption in the world. [[Carnalix]] are drawn into frenzy by the smell of blood, and [[Lyd, The First Beloved]] was no exception. But where other [[Carnalix]] become hungry, [[Lyd, The First Beloved]] became obsessed. It did not merely seek blood. It sought the blood of the Fox. Or what it thought was the Fox.

The instant it catches that scent—fox-fur, fox-blood, fox-absence, the sharp edge of a threshold about to open—it changes. The beloved face is still there for a breath.

Then the hunting body wakes.

The amber eyes sharpen. The antlers angle forward like horns of pursuit. The lark-song becomes a shriek of location and alarm. The cat's paws dig in. The wolf-thread seizes command. The horse-thread drives the body forward with terrible speed. The whole creature becomes a stalking engine made of devotion and hunger.

This is the true horror of [[Lyd, The First Beloved]]. It is not passive ruin. It is an active predator of endings. It hunts across [[Leylines]], through abandoned thresholds, into ritual spaces, into places where [[Strand]] might briefly be close enough to smell. It tears apart false foxes, illusions, masks, bloodied remnants, and the traces of any creature that carries even a suggestion of release. It does not understand mercy as a thing separate from the prey. It only understands that the fox-shaped thing is the only thing it can never digest.

And so it yearns for that blood.

Not to consume the Fox as food.

To force [[Strand]] to become flesh.

To make the missing Weight bleed.

To make the absence answer.

### The Manifestation of the [[Interregnum]]

The [[Interregnum]] is the first monstrous manifestation of [[Lyd, The First Beloved]]—the outer catastrophe that appears before the beloved form can properly assemble. It is what happens when too much suffering, too much grafting of body parts, and too much biomagical alteration force the creature to manifest before it can fully resolve into the seven parts that make the true creature.

At first, it is not clearly a body at all. It appears as a puddle of [[Formless Masses]]—a black-and-red wet collapse of residue pooled together at the site of accumulated damage. But within that ruin something pale begins to rise, a second shape hidden inside the puddle: a seed, visibly rotting, swollen with impossible life, and unmistakably distinct from the mass around it. It is the first true sign that the creature is trying to become itself. Half-organ, half-embryo, half-wound, it pulses like something trying to hatch while already decaying.

The seed does not remain still. As it hardens and grows, it sheds new puddles of [[Formless Masses]] around itself. These spread outward in trembling slicks, each one thick with failed matter, lingering pain, and half-separated flesh. The ground around the [[Interregnum]] becomes stained with these lesser collapses, and from them rise many lesser [[Carnalix Atonalis]], drawn to the excess suffering and unfinished body that produced them.

It grows until it becomes the size of a cathedral.

The [[Interregnum]] is not a creature in the way the [[Beloved Shards]] or the seven parts are creatures. It is a highly anomalous object—a structure that operates by irradiation rather than action, producing harm not through behavior but through existence. The correct comparison is not to a predator. It is to a radioactive material that causes cancer and tumours not because it attacks, but because it is constitutively, permanently wrong in a way that the surrounding matter cannot accommodate.

The [[Interregnum]] exists in a state of permanent stasis—an egg that cannot hatch because it has not yet gathered enough suffering to do so, and cannot stop drawing suffering to itself because that is what its architecture does. The mycelium-like structures that extend from its base—pale, wet, thread-thin, spreading through soil and stone and compressed [[Leylines]] residue—are not roots in any botanical sense. They are the weave reaching.

The [[Interregnum]] is the weave's attempt to hold itself together before the creature is ready to be born, and it holds itself together the same way [[Lyd, The First Beloved]] has always held itself together: by incorporating what surrounds it. Over time, everything within the [[Interregnum]]'s radial reach begins to decay in the specific way the weave decays—not rapidly, not cleanly, but in the manner of something that cannot be shed. Plants rot without dying. Animals develop chronic conditions without cause. Beings experience the subjective sensation of accumulation: old injuries that resurface, sorrows that should have passed that instead deepen.

The mycelium extracts this decay and feeds it to the central egg, and the egg grows heavier, and the seam at its center strains harder, and the day it finally hatches draws incrementally closer.

This is why the [[Interregnum]] cannot be moved. It is not that the object is too heavy, though at full development it may cover territory that dwarfs a city. It is that the [[Interregnum]]'s mycelium has threaded itself through everything that is decaying within range, and decay is everywhere. To move it is to rupture it—and rupture does not stop the process. It releases the [[Beloved Shards]] before the egg is ready, scatters the accumulated suffering back into the [[Leylines]] as concentrated [[Dissonance]], and accelerates every stage that follows.

The egg, intact, is the only containment that exists.

And it is fragile.

And it is filling.

At a distance, it looks like a large ovoid shape rising from a pool of [[Formless Masses]]. Its final form is pale and swollen, standing in the landscape like a thing that should not be upright at all. The body is disturbingly smooth in some places and ragged in others, a patchwork of flesh, bone, and half-healed tissue stretched over a shape that feels assembled rather than born. The outer surface has the soft, bruised look of overripe flesh, but beneath that softness are rigid ribs pressing outward in long vaulted arcs, as though a rib cage had grown around a womb and forgotten which of them was meant to contain the other.

In its closed phase, the [[Interregnum]] appears almost sealed. A vertical central seam runs through the middle of the body like a wound held shut by force rather than healing. The line is too neat to be natural and too wet to be dead, a dark slit in the pale mass that trembles with the pressure behind it. From far away it reads like a folded organ, an embryonic sac, a body trying desperately to keep itself from splitting open. Up close, the seam is ringed with tender-looking tissue and faint ridges of scar-flesh, as though the whole thing has been stitched together from suffering and is still straining against the stitches.

It continues to produce [[Formless Masses]] and lesser [[Carnalix Atonalis]] until it is attacked.

When someone ruptures the outer layer, it does not remain closed for long.

As the pressure inside builds, the seam begins to part. The two sides of the body draw back from each other in a slow, obscene opening, like a seedpod splitting or a birth canal forced wide. What was hidden inside is revealed in a wet, pulsing exposure: a deeper inner mass, red and slick and still beating, half embryo and half organ, nested in the ruined architecture of ribs and flesh.

The opening is not clean. It tears along old graft-lines, peeling the body open in layered folds, and the release is accompanied by the smell of blood, heat, rot, and disturbed earth. The whole object throbs as if it is breathing through pain.

The opening and closing are not separate motions so much as phases of the same failure: first containment, then rupture; first the sealed body, then the exposed core. It is not yet a creature in the proper sense. It is a body trying to become one, and showing its mistake in two stages. Womb, rib, embryo, ruin. A cathedral-sized body built around a seed that is rotting while it grows.

It manifests its own [[Dissonance Core]] in that exposed core, prompting it to be slain.

When this manifested body is slain, it decays and sheds. The preserved flesh and incorporated matter sloughs away. The absorbed stones and [[Leylines]] residue release back into the ground. Centuries of accumulated damage return to the world as [[Dissonance]], seeding new lesser [[Carnalix Atonalis]] along the [[Leylines]] near where it fell. The incorporated creatures inside the walls dissolve back into [[Formless Masses]] and scatter.

What the shedding reveals—the last thing, the deepest thing, the seed inside the massive carcass—are The Seven Parts and the Six Woven Weights.

These fragments do not remain inert.

They become [[Beloved Shards]].

### The Comforting [[Beloved Shards]]

Small, cat-sized, warm fragments of [[Lyd, The First Beloved]] that wander the world attached to refused endings. They curl at bedsides, on graves, in abandoned nurseries, in rooms left exactly as they were after a death. They sit beside widows who refuse to clear the chair. They sleep beside books no one reads anymore. They knead the floorboards of houses where someone still sets two plates.

They are comforting.

That is the terrible part.

They are the body of [[Lyd, The First Beloved]] reduced to tenderness, and their tenderness is how they spread. The older the refusal, the more likely a Shard is to stay. The more the blood it smells resembles the Fox, the more likely it is to go feral.

The animals that appear beside the dying, the grieving, and the chronically suffering are not a coincidence of nature. They are [[Beloved Shards]]—byproducts of [[Lyd, The First Beloved]]'s own slow decay, fragments of [[Corded Flesh]] and accumulated purpose shed from the [[Interregnum]]'s outer body as it absorbs and sheds the rot of its surrounding environment. They do not choose to comfort. They are drawn. The suffering body produces [[Corded Flesh]], and corded flesh is food. The Shard arrives the way a fungus arrives at a wound—not out of mercy, but out of appetite and resonance.

What makes this horror elegant is its disguise. The [[Beloved Shard]] is warm. It presses close. It kneads. It stays through the night when no one else will. Hospitals, death-chambers, gravesites—these are simply the places where corded flesh concentrates most densely, where the [[Leylines]] carry the most accumulated suffering, where the Shard can feed while performing the function it was woven to perform.

The presence of [[Lyd, The First Beloved]], even in its most diminished form, does not cause suffering.

It sustains it.

Every creature that curls beside a dying body and is called a comfort is making that death slightly more permanent. The Shard eats. The body holds on a little longer. And the Shard grows.

When the host finally dies, the Shard does not leave.

It consumes.

Each fragment of [[Lyd, The First Beloved]] grows on the corpse of the [[Corded Flesh]] it has cultivated—patient, faithful, satisfied in the way the cat was always satisfied—and carries the accumulated damage of that refused ending forward into its next host. This is why [[Beloved Shards]] found near long-term hospices or ancient tombs are larger and more wrong than those found near fresh grief. They have been eating for longer.

What looks like an animal staying with the dying is not loyalty to the dying.

It is the weave recognizing a rich harvest and refusing to let it go to waste.

There is a brief moment after the shedding and before the reunion—quiet, easy to miss—when the world can breathe. The old pain eases. Bodies that had been archiving instead of shedding begin, briefly, to process what they could not process before.

It lasts until the first two Parts find each other.

Then it ends.

### The Seven Parts

When the outer mass sheds, the seven [[Beloved Shards]] begin hunting and growing, changing from pet-sized forms into enormous, monstrous, separate creatures—each one carrying the full weight of the quality it was woven to embody, each one incomplete without the others, each one drawn by the pull of [[The First Overtone]] threads toward reunion.

**The Wolf-That-Stays** emerges enormous, grey-silver, scar-layered, with the sharp forward muzzle of the original [[Lyd, The First Beloved]] grown vast and the amber eyes still directly, faithfully oriented at a frequency the world cannot see. It does not hunt prey. It hunts departure. It finds whoever carries the scent of a final goodbye and follows them until the goodbye is broken.

**The Deer-of-No-Endings** emerges with antler structures grown to architectural proportion, the oldest tines black and necrotic at the tips, new growth still pale from the base. Its antler-cathedral is not empty. The interior corridors are narrow and ribbed, with walls of scar-bone that flex when the body breathes. Embedded in those corridors are preserved silhouettes of prior refusals—a child frozen mid-turn, a pair of hands still reaching toward a closed door, a collar fused into the flesh of a passage. They are not skeletons. They are holdings.

**The Lark-of-Unfinished-Song** emerges still bright, still quick, still singing, its little throat pouring out impossible morning notes from a body that has no morning left in it. Dead for longer than memory but still moving. It is the most beautiful and most unbearable of the Parts, because its joy was never malicious, only preserved too long. Objects it touches are preserved in a state of almost-bloom, never fully breaking, never fully being allowed to complete their cycle. Its melody is the [[Lydian Cadence]], and those who hear it near an ending never know whether they have been comforted or condemned.

**The Cat-of-Persisting-Silence** emerges with its delicate forepaws multiplied, extra digits folded in on each other, claws that no longer fully retract, still moving with the unmistakable kneading of contentment at a scale that makes the gesture wrong. It appears beside the dying, the preserved, the tended. Those who touch it carry the memory of the texture for days—a phantom sensation of something both soft and wrong.

**The Horse-of-Carried-Weight** emerges as the largest Part, walking with the gait of something bearing weight too long to remember movement without it. Its structural core is the most visible expression of the horse's [[Weight of Nature]]—massive, honest, occupying space as a statement of existence, carrying all the accumulated mass of what could not be set down. Bodies near it begin to feel their physical nature as burden rather than form—somatic symptoms without organic cause, the weight of essential self made into pressure.

**The Rabbit-of-Unfinished-Becoming** emerges as a creature of impossible softness grown monstrous—the white of its coat still perfect in patches, the rest grey and accumulated, its tail still the most heartbreaking detail on the body, still perfectly, unbearably soft. It moves through places where futures were prevented. Near it, the body begins to produce [[Corded Flesh]] specifically in the systems of unrealized growth—the muscle that never built, the strength that was never permitted to develop, the potential that was preserved at an insufficient stage.

The Fox does not emerge from the [[Corpus Mortuum]] because it was never inside it. It appears at the edge of the reunion site, as it always does, watching.

And if you watch where it steps, the ground is wet.

### The Reunion and the Hunt

The six Parts find each other the way old wounds find each other—drawn by resonance, by the frequency of accumulated damage only they share, toward the same places: thresholds, refused endings, the geography of things kept going past their time. When all six are in contact, pressing against each other with the warmth of animals that have been separated and know the difference, the weave reconnects.

Simultaneously, the six Woven Weights—Purpose, Value, Flaw, Indulgence, Nature, Potential—have been circling the world since the shedding, each a small principle carrying only itself, incomplete. When the six Parts reconnect, the six Weights are drawn to the reunion and the [[Beloved Kernel]] forms: the complete interior of [[Lyd, The First Beloved]] before its outer flesh, the philosophical core from which the [[Lyd, The First Beloved]] will hatch in its true form.

The [[Seventh]] Weight—Change, the Fox—stands at the edge of the [[Beloved Kernel]]'s formation as it always does. It watches the architecture of [[Lyd, The First Beloved]]'s identity complete itself with the fox-shaped absence at its center. It feels the weave reach for it.

It walks away, as it always does.

And [[Lyd, The First Beloved]] lunges.

That is the moment the cycle becomes violent again.

The [[Beloved Kernel]] hatches. The six Parts fold into each other, threading back together from the level of [[The First Overtone]] threads, becoming the single small body they were woven to be.

The rabbit's tail, white and perfect.

The deer's velvet antler-buds, warm to the touch.

The wolf's forward-pointing muzzle and amber eyes still looking for her.

The cat's forepaws already beginning to knead.

The horse's deep chest, solid and warm.

The lark's bright throat already beginning to sing.

And the fox-shaped space at the center of all of it, where change was always supposed to be, where change will never be, where the capacity to end and begin again was absent from the first weaving and will be absent from every weaving after.

[[Lyd, The First Beloved]] is born.

Again.

Still without Change.

Still waiting for her.

Still hunting what it can never eat.

Still the most faithful thing she ever made.

entries.title: Magic Arts
entries.summary: The applications of [[Spellweaving]] based on [[The Registers of Magic]] and how they are grouped based on common ground, purpose, or manipulation methods of a specific binding.
entries.body:
The applications of [[Spellweaving]] based on [[The Registers of Magic]] and how they are grouped based on common ground, purpose, or manipulation methods of a specific binding. These range from using the same principle of [[Resonance Field]]s, such as [[Field Magic]], or utilizing a similar niche like [[Nimbus Arts]] which are focused on creating many types of miniature clouds, and similar concentrations of [[Flux]] through the imbuing of [[Cindergale]] momentum and energy to create a direct stream of droplets that deliver the payload through rain.

The divisions of [[Magic Arts]] are either:

- Registers of Magic: The broad applications that are called magic instead of arts such as [[Wind Magic]], [[Fire Magic]], [[Illusory Magic]], [[Dream Magic]], [[Prism Magic]], [[Liminal Magic]], [[Mortuary Magic]], etc.
- Subsets of Magic: The subdivisions of a branch of magic that encompass entire applications of [[Magic Arts]] such as [[Zephyr Arts]], [[Breathing Arts]], [[Psychic Arts]], [[Ink Arts]], [[Celestial Holography Arts]], [[Dimensional Arts]], [[Magnetism Arts]], [[Cryomagic Arts]], [[Hyperphantasia Arts]], etc.
- Niches of Magic: Individual applications for a very specific function, purpose, or utilizing a specific application of a subset, such as [[Snow Arts]] being part of [[Cryomagic Arts]] or [[Ornamental Gardening Arts]] being part of [[Agromagical Arts]]. Very specific ones function as advanced magic such as the [[Hollow-Point]], [[Warp Travel Arts]], [[Entropic Scrying Arts]], [[Fire Funnel Arts]], or [[Butterfly Web Arts]].

For example, a very unique niche are [[Perfumery Arts]] ([[Flux]] + [[Resonance]] + [[Cindergale]]) which are a niche of scent-crafting and emotional influence through volatile essences, and rely on creating mist or cloud-like structures for a [[Resonance Field]] of chemical and magical compounds.

These can be used in its basic to create perfumes from [[Emotional Residue]] but for combat they are useful to imbue with other properties such as flammability to create a mist of aromatic signatures that diffuse emotional carriers, enable [[Stable Harmonic Channels]] for follow-up spells or to make the target enter a trigger of [[Sympathetic Vibration]].

This niche is found within [[Transmutation Arts]] ([[Flux]] + [[Crystal]] + [[Resonance]]) which are the subset of alchemical practice of changing the material state, substance or condition through one another by using the dynamism of [[Flux]]. While the broader register is [[Liminal Magic]] ([[Flux]] + [[Resonance]]) which is one of the applications of the Tessitura of [[Flux]].
entries.source: Worldbuilding/World Environment/Atonalis/Spellweaving Rituals/Magic Arts.md

entries.title: Memory Field
entries.summary: An advanced type of a [[Strand Pool]] mirroring as an archeomagical [[Strand]] field that contain the weight of history for a strong event. It's the result of [[Echoing Bonds]] imprinted on the place of occurrence.
entries.body:
An advanced type of a [[Strand Pool]] mirroring as an archeomagical [[Strand]] field that contain the weight of history for a strong event. It's the result of [[Echoing Bonds]] imprinted on the place of occurrence.

It exhibits similar properties to that of a [[Strand Pool]]:

- Temporal Distortion: Time flows irregularly, a visitor can feel the experience of hours passing yet emerge to find only minutes have passed, or vice versa.
- [[Object Permanence]] at Large Scale: They maintain a blueprint of historical data of how something, someone, or somewhere used to be in the past on a vast field.

However, [[Memory Field]]s are [[Strand Pool]]s strong enough to be outside the [[Trinity Harmony]]'s normal temporal current, being looped instead with the specific moment its standing-wave crystalized into [[Resonance]].

They also preserve an oddly quiet aura with only a gentle wind that filters all exterior sound. Such is the primary indicator that the [[Strand Pool]] is a [[Memory Field]]. This phenomenon occurs due to the time-dilated presence of static of [[Primal White Noise]], nullifying most of the outside [[Resonance]], and preserving only a muted atmosphere of the historical event.

Surprisingly, [[Memory Field]]s are sites of high [[Coherence]], even if the surrounding environment is filled with [[Static Criticality]] or [[Dissonance]], they're the very "eye of the hurricane" for magic.

### Canon [[Memory Field]]s:

Depending on the [[Ages]] some [[Memory Field]]s appear in [[Arcanoria]] as specific spots within the map. All the list considers:

- Unnamed Harbor: The ruined version of [[Lune Shallow]] after [[A Pact of a Thousand Eyes]] has been completed and [[The Hollowing]] begins. It contains the story of [[Mira]] and the [[Ballad]] of the Girl Left Behind.
- [[The Silent Expanse]] Epicenter: Atop the cliff where [[The Auric Aria's Suicide]] happened in the first field of [[Forsaken Flower]]s. It contains the story of the [[Eighth Cycle]] and the truth about the [[Auric Aria]] descent.
entries.source: Worldbuilding/World Environment/Landmarks/Memory Field.md

entries.title: Minor Note
entries.summary: [[Minor Note]]s draw upon fleeting emotions and lighter expressions of elemental power; they are most suitable for simple charms but most commonly used in supportive enhancement effects.
entries.body:
[[Minor Note]]s draw upon fleeting emotions and lighter expressions of elemental power; they are most suitable for simple charms but most commonly used in supportive enhancement effects.

Though [[Minor Note]] spells cost little, usually only slight fatigue, even the most trivial enchantment can ascend to a [[Major Note]] when it's fueled by a significant and meaningful [[Essence Sacrifice]].

- The [[Dual Confluence Stream]] ([[Lunehymn]] + [[Aetherlight]]) runs weak, snarled, and uneven.
- The great agricultural rites of prior Ages—growth hymns, irrigation chords, soil‑healing Ornaments—are gone or reduced to half‑remembered myths.
- Magic in this age is mostly **[[Minor Note]] instinct**:
    - A spark coaxed from damp wood.
    - A wound closed by desperate humming.
    - An arrow guided a hair’s breadth truer.
entries.source: Worldbuilding/Origin of Magic/The Principles of Magic.md; Worldbuilding/Rise & Fall, Crisis/Crisis/The Inescapable Hunger.md

### [[Memory Field]]: The Girl Left Behind That Changed a God

**[[Ballad]] Fragment Introduction. The Girl Left Behind**

The memory comes to [[Mira]] in fragments, like trying to reconstruct something from salt and ash.

She remembers a man’s hands—calloused, stained, trembling. She remembers being lifted, and the weight of that lifting. She remembers the smell of sickness and the ocean, mingled together so entirely that she can never separate them.

She remembers the sound of him weeping. But also the sweet sound of a gentle lullaby washed by the waves.

A sickly father—ravaged by a consumption that the healers in the mountain villages had no names for—walked three days down from the high country to reach [[Lune Shallow]]. He did not come for healing. He came because he was dying, and he knew it, and he needed one thing before the end: he needed his daughter to live.

The fisherman who found her on the dock that morning was named [[Kael]]. He was alone — his wife had died in childbirth years before, and he had learned to accept the silence of his home as the price of avoiding the pain of sharing it. Lovestruck and still grieving, yet he knew the sea had few space left for spared tears.

But he couldn't bear the sight of a child left at the dock, of a child wrapped in cloth expensive once yet now threadbare, with a letter that simply read: *“Her name is [[Mira]]. Her father is dead. Her mother is dead. Save her. She deserves the world. —A Father’s Last Act”* — a child like that could not be left alone.

And so, he took [[Mira]] under his care.

[[Kael]] later told people he did not decide to raise her. He just did not choose not to. And by the time he was aware of the decision that had been made, [[Mira]] was already 3 years old and calling him "Father."

**[[Ballad]] Fragment I. An Ill-Stricken Orphan**

For most of [[Mira]]'s childhood, [[Lune Shallow]] was a place of relative peace. The Second Wave of the [[Great Plague]] had ravaged many settlements, but it had largely spared the secluded bay, and the fisherman raised her as his father had raised him— with work, with expectation, with the kind of love that is expressed through action rather than softness.

[[Kael]] was also a careful man; he had grown cold since the passing of his wife, yet he still kept memory of them, and saw a home in everything [[Mira]] did — in the way she moved, the way she grew, and in the way she delighted in savoring sweets every so often. However, his work, while simple, required dedication. For most dawns he would be leaving early their home until night came. Yet he would not leave [[Mira]] unattended on his house. On the contrary, he would often take her with him to the docks, but this wouldn't last long.

The cough came the year she turned 8. It started as a tickle. Then a persistent rattle in her chest. Until one sunset, when [[Kael]] was securing his ship after work's end on the harbor with [[Mira]]'s help, it deeply worsened.

It was close to nightfall, and both [[Mira]] and [[Kael]] were about to finish a long day of work. They were each on opposite sides of the deck, anchoring the mast of a wooden vessel. [[Mira]] pulled the line taut, made two passes, and [[Kael]] was waiting for her to secure the line, but before she made the third pass her lungs faltered.

A deep cough bent her double.

It felt like something inside her was trying to escape her throat, and by the time it had passed, her hands had lost the strength required to keep the boat steady, and the grip pulled her to the cold sea.

[[Kael]] lunged immediately to the waves to rescue her. [[Mira]] was fighting as much the cough anew as she was trying not to drown.

Once washed ashore, [[Mira]] was trembling but without signs of any major injury. In a sigh of relief [[Kael]] kept her in a tight embrace. Delicately streaking the sides of her hair, humming the familiar lullaby that would calm [[Mira]].

It had been a long time since the fisherman ever took care of someone like this. His heart never fully healed from the loss of a possible family cut short, yet the sight of [[Mira]] in his embrace was the reflection of the home he would vow to never lose again.

The truth was, he could not call her "daughter." The word caught in his throat — not from rejection, but from the weight it carried. To say "daughter" was to name what he'd failed to protect. So instead, [[Kael]] found smaller names, and gentler approaches. He found ways to speak his love that didn't require him to speak his loss.

And to protect [[Mira]] as much as it was to protect himself, it would become the language of their entire life together.

The incident was as much of a toll for [[Mira]] as it was for [[Kael]]. [[Mira]] had learned that her body wasn't fully hers. The frailty of her lungs was the only inheritance her biological family had left. And for [[Kael]], it was the wake-up call to the delicate thread that kept their home alive.

From now onwards, he would leave [[Mira]] on her own while he went fishing, as an act of love to protect her from the strains of physical labor and the toll of her condition.

The routine changed slowly, then all at once. [[Mira]] used to spend the entire day at the docks by his side. Now the mornings belonged to the silence of the house when [[Kael]] went off at sunrise.

At first she still tried to help. She sometimes carried water from the nearby well on top of the harbor's hill to help [[Kael]] with the morning routine. But one time too often would the bucket’s handle bite into her fingers, until halfway home her hands began to shake.

One morning as her cough rose, raw and tearing. The water spilled into the dirt in a dark fan when she was close to home. [[Kael]] came out at the sound, took the bucket from her without rebuke, and carried it inside himself.

Another [[Moon]], [[Mira]] tried to mend nets alone one afternoon while [[Kael]] was still away. The twine blurred when the coughing fit came; her fingers lost their rhythm. When [[Kael]] returned, he found the net tangled in her lap and her chest heaving as she forced shallow breaths between spasms.

He did not scold her then either. He sat beside her and untangled the net in silence, his jaw tight with a heavy heart.

After that, [[Kael]] stopped asking her to help with work that demanded strength.

Instead, she watched.

Often she would stroll alongside [[Lune Shallow]]'s market, harbor, and the docks where her biological father had left her. It wasn't long before [[Mira]] learned which fishermen came back with their shoulders heavy. She also came to recognize which merchants lied by watching their hands instead of their mouths, and she became skilled at reading the gait of the few spare widows who moved as if the air itself pressed against them.

While [[Mira]] felt the weight of being by herself, [[Kael]] in turn however, would make it up by showing her love through teaching her skills he had learned on the waves whenever he came back from a fishing trip.

He feared hurting her as much as he feared neglecting his own role as a father.

Thus, [[Mira]] learned to mend nets in the evenings, when breathing was easier and the air smelled of salt and cooked fish rather than murk and wet rope. She learned to read the [[Moon]]'s phases and their effect on the tides. She knew the taste of salt, the color of different depths, the way the harbor changed with the seasons.

But perhaps the most important lesson was what [[Kael]] told her one sunset while they mended the nets together.

He now reached consistently to one of those smaller names — the one that had become his language for loving her when "daughter" was too heavy.

"What is it, sweet tooth?" [[Kael]] said in a soft, raspy voice when he noticed her oblivious gaze into the horizon. "You look as lost as the barnacles washed ashore."

"You forgot how to tie the ends? We can go over knots again if you're unsure," [[Kael]] said jokingly, expecting a response from [[Mira]] but she kept a stare to herself.

"I'll treat you something sweet nice after we head to the market tonight," [[Kael]] proposed while throwing a net to catch [[Mira]]'s attention. "Merchant supplies are ever running dry with the [[Great Plague]] but with today's catch we can afford a few luxuries. Maybe even one or two of those breads you like a lot—"

"Father, why can't I be with you?" [[Mira]] replied quietly with tears building on the rim of her eyes.

"Ah, that's what it is," [[Kael]] let out a deep sigh while trying to make up the words as he scratches the top of his forehead. "You know what happened last time. I would like to take you with me sweet tooth, but hard labor is not for you. And that's not all there is to work, tracking the [[Moon]] is much more important than reeling the fish."

"You always say that, but what if you don't come back..." [[Mira]]'s tears began to run down her cheeks while sobbing. "I... miss you. And if I'm alone..."

[[Kael]] dropped the net to cut her sentence short.

"[[Mira]], I will never leave you. Not this [[Moon]], nor the next, nor for a thousand [[Cycle]]s," [[Kael]] said to reassure her in his still raspy voice. "Just like your father does, I also live in you, in your memory, in your emotions. Even in the tears that run down your cheeks, if you can feel me. I'm here."

"Even if you can't look at this sack of rags." [[Kael]] laughed while removing his coat.

"And that's the truth, [[Mira]]. I can't always be here next to you, but I don't really leave if you can say I'm still here," [[Kael]] says as he puts his coat on top of [[Mira]]'s shoulders as a sort of hug, "You're a smart young lady, and there's plenty of things you can do by observing the world on your own."

"People are just like schools of fish, and are always trying to hide," he would say while pointing at the [[Leylines]] converging with the rivers at the shore, "but if you watch long enough, you can see what they're protecting. And sometimes, if you're with them, they'll let you be a witness to it."

"I'm sure you're already better than me at that just by watching everyone on [[Lune Shallow]]'s harbor." [[Kael]] continued while trying to ease the tension. "I'd be real lucky if I could watch through a merchant's tricks."

[[Mira]] did not understand what he meant at the time. But those words kept in her mind as much as the sound of the washing waves.

"I'm sorry you can't accompany me anymore, [[Mira]] but I too have something to protect," [[Kael]] continues in a somber yet jokingly way while closing the leather of his coat now covering [[Mira]], "I wouldn't want any more salt on your tangled little hair. It's hard enough to comb it as it is."

[[Kael]] then carried [[Mira]] on his shoulders, heading to the market in the hope to lift up her spirits with as many sweets as his pockets would allow. It wasn't the first nor the last time [[Mira]] would struggle with loss and her worth. [[Kael]] himself recognized that she seemed to carry something heavy even as a child, though he never quite found the words to ask about it.

He instead taught her that to be present is much more important than longing in the past. And to help her with such, he guided [[Mira]] to notice things in others the same way he saw them in her.

**[[Ballad]] Fragment II. The Departure**

A few years went by. [[Mira]], now grown to the age of 12, picked up on the habit of being the lookout for [[Lune Shallow]]'s gathering caravans on the harbor's [[Trade Node]] when [[Kael]] was gone.

The few times that a merchant arrived to a [[Secluded Refuge]] such as [[Lune Shallow]], they were always met with skepticism as a threat to the population. The Second Wave of the [[Great Plague]] had taught many to distrust anyone coming from outside. Horror stories travelled all throughout [[Arcanoria]] of a dancing frenzy that would never cease until it consumed everything.

Perhaps it was blind luck or the secluded location of the settlement, but for the people of [[Lune Shallow]] it was because the [[Moon]] watched over them. The folk story was that the [[Lunehymn]] that flowed from the [[Leylines]] here was imbued with a blessing of the heavens themselves.

One autumn, a merchant caravan from the southern pass arrived later than expected, its wagons rimed with dust and its people moving with the wary stiffness of those who had seen too many sickbeds. Among them was a boy around [[Mira]]'s age, with sun‑bleached hair and a gap in him carrying losses she recognized but could not name.

His name was Kyrie, although [[Mira]] later adopted a nickname of her own: [[Kyvy]].

He stayed with one of the miller families at the edge of the village, a household that had taken him in after his own had been lost somewhere along the southern roads across the great mountains that separate [[Lune Shallow]] from the [[Great Plague]].

[[Mira]] first saw him by the tide rocks, throwing pebbles into the water with the same absent focus she had once used on knots.

They did not speak at first. They simply threw stones together and watched the circles expand, collide, and vanish in [[Resonance]]. But the repeating appearance of [[Kyvy]] on the docks while [[Kael]] was away planted the seeds of her first friendship.

In later weeks, [[Kyvy]] showed [[Mira]] how to whistle with a blade of seagrass. She brought him peppermint leaves from [[Kael]]'s small garden. And they tend to talk about the few things they both knew about the sea — the color of the sky before storms, the way gulls cried like lost children, how the cold made the murk and water clearer.

With [[Kyvy]], [[Mira]] was not [[Lune Shallow]]'s sick girl or the fisherman’s foundling. She was just a girl who knew the tides better than he did, who could point out which clouds meant weather, who laughed when his whistling attempts failed.

It was the first thing in her life she had taken for herself instead of being given.

However, when she mentioned [[Kyvy]] in a conversation over diner, [[Kael]]'s hands stilled briefly over his bowl.

"That caravan of millers came from the south pass," he said. "From the villages that are now lost to most maps."

"[[Kyvy]] said his family died in a mudslide," [[Mira]] answered.

"Mudslides follow storms as sure as the [[Great Plague]] follows people," [[Kael]] muttered, then shook his head, as if scolding his own thoughts. "It's great that you've finally made friends but just promise me to be careful, sweet tooth."

[[Mira]] continued to exchange time with [[Kyvy]] for the following next four [[Moon]]s while [[Kael]] was gone until dusk. She now had built on the habit to visit the home of [[Kyvy]] in the outskirts of [[Lune Shallow]].

One dreaded morning, however, the miller’s house stood empty.

The door was open with leftover ashes on a cold hearth. A few chairs layed overturned in the yard. Inside, the bedding of the rooms was gone. Only in the middle of the floor sat by the fire a small wooden windpipe, its edges rough-carved, as if it was made in a hurry.

[[Mira]] stood in the doorway, first calling awkwardly for [[Kyvy]], then for any names, until at last she tried to scream in a breath thin and fast. Her cough scratched at her throat, but she held it back for finding anyone was more important than tending to herself.

Desperately, she looked on every house of the neighboring caravan but she was only met with the deafening silence of absence until the sun fell down.

[[Kyvy]] was gone. No note. No farewell. No presence of himself or his adopted family.

[[Mira]] ran back toward the harbor when last streaks of sunlight set by the horizon of the sea beyond the empty houses. Her lungs were burning from the physical strain after desperate hours of searching. Ultimately, she was met by no one until she found [[Kael]] at the docks, mending nets alone.

"[[Kael]]! They left!" she said, the words catching between coughs. "The caravan, the millers. [[Kyvy]] — he's gone!"

[[Kael]]'s hands froze in the net. For a moment, his face didn’t move at all, as if skipping a breath. Then something sharp passed behind his eyes. He set the net aside very carefully, as if it were something that might break.

"You went to their house?" he asked, too quietly.

"He’s my friend," [[Mira]] said, as if that explained everything.

"[[Mira]]," [[Kael]] began, but whatever softer word he had been reaching for turned to stone on his tongue. "Those people... They came from the [[Great Plague]]. They knew it. They knew all the stories. They came here anyway and then left in the night."

He stood, his voice rising now, hoarse with something like panic. "You’ve been coughing around them. You’ve been in their house, breathing their air! And now they’re gone! Do you understand what that looks like? To them? To the rest of the village?"

Tears burned at the corners of [[Mira]]’s eyes. "He wouldn’t leave without saying goodbye."

"He didn’t have a choice!" [[Kael]] finally snapped. "They left because they were afraid. Afraid of what follows them, afraid of what follows you. In the end they all leave! Whether by choice or by force... That’s why we don’t tie ourselves to people who can disappear with the next tide."

He had never raised his voice at her like that. The words hit harder than the cold water ever had.

"[[Mira]], I have told you many times! We are safe because we are forgotten," he continued, voice fraying. "[[Lune Shallow]] only survived so far because no one thinks of us. The moment people remember us, they bring their plagues and their fear and their leaving. And we are the ones who stay with whatever they’ve stirred up."

[[Mira]] said nothing. She could not tell where his anger ended and his fear began. She tried to compose herself but no words could come from the knot of her throat.

"Don’t ask the world for things it cannot keep," [[Kael]] now with his voice wore down to a rasp concluded, "If you don't want to meaningless suffer then don’t cling to what can disappear before the end of the night..."

[[Kael]] finally stopped with a deep breath, and turned back to the nets. He couldn't keep the sight of her daughter crying of the pain of loss. [[Kael]] knew he should comfort her, but her wound mirrored too close to his own. So he kept on working, with his fingers moving faster than before, as if mending rope could keep anything else from coming apart.

That night a deep silence covered their house, [[Mira]] lay awake listening to the waves and to her own lungs drag air in and out of her chest. She didn’t know whether the caravan and [[Kyvy]] had left because of her, or because of something beyond the horizon, but the knot between those possibilities tightened around her ribs all the same.

She did not ask [[Kael]] if he thought she was to blame. She did not ask if he would ever leave without saying goodbye. She did not ask for anything anymore.

In the [[Moon]]s that followed, [[Kael]] tried, clumsily, to soften what he had said.

He brought her honey cakes from the market on days even when the catch wasn't good. He returned from longer trips with little things in his pockets — smooth stones, a strip of colored cloth, a tarnished coin from some other, larger harbor.

"[[Mira]]," he said one dawn before he left to work, his voice careful, "about what I said. About them leaving because of you. I was afraid. I spoke badly. I… I didn’t mean to put all of that on your shoulders."

"It’s fine," [[Mira]] answered, eyes on her hands.

"Sweet tooth, it’s not fine," [[Kael]] said, sharper than he intended. Then, softer: "I can see it’s not. You haven’t asked me for anything since."

She thought about denying it, but that would have been another kind of lie.

Instead, [[Mira]] reflected on that nickname. She had never given second thought to what [[Kael]] called her, but then she remembered the one name she herself gave to [[Kyvy]]. This time "Sweet tooth" felt hollow.

"You're still calling me that?," she said instead and continued after a sigh. "You’re a good father. You saved me. You feed me. That’s enough."

"[[Mira]], I don’t want ‘enough’ from you," he whispered. "I want you to know you can ask. For sweets, for time, for… whatever you need— You're my daughter..."

[[Mira]] was surprised to hear those words coming from him. It filled a [[Void]] she had been yearning for. But then the memories of the day she was abandoned at the docks flooded her.

She shook her head and in a soft voice she replied, "Every time I’ve wanted something, it’s gone. Or it hurts. Or it leaves. It’s easier to let go."

[[Kael]] looked at her then with an expression of grief that hurt her as much as she wished to deny it to the point that [[Mira]] had to look away.

"Did— Did I do that to you?," he said in a voice close to breaking.

She did not contradict him. There was nothing kind to say that would also be true.

The only words [[Mira]] could phrase were: "I still love you, Father. And that's enough."

**[[Ballad]] Fragment III. The Third Wave**

By age 19, [[Mira]] came to the cruelest realization yet, the sickly condition she had since inherited from her bygone family since her childhood rapidly worsened into what would be finally her end.

It started on the morning where she was awakened from her sleep by a feeling of suffocation. For a moment [[Mira]] believed it was a dream where she was drowning, as one of the nightmares that haunted her every so often about being left at the mercy of the waves, but it quickly came to her senses that she was in her home.

She curled up to the side of the bed, and the moment she fully realized she was awake, she coughed a pool of blood.

[[Kael]] quickly came to her room after hearing the noise of the desperate thrashing.

He froze at the scene the moment he saw the position [[Mira]] was in, for he knew what this meant. He had watched the Second Wave claim victims the same way.

He did not speak of it.

Instead, he held her hand more often, softly but desperately clinging to her touch. He sat with her through the nights when her cough was worst. And when she asked him, "[[Kael]], am I going to die as my family did?" he did not lie to her.

"Yes," he said with a heavy heart. "Probably. But not today. And that's the only promise anyone has."

It was not cruel, this honesty. It was, in its own way, the most incredible kindness because it allowed [[Mira]] to stop being afraid and start being present to her own life.

She began leaving the house more deliberately, not out of rebellion against her body's limitations, but because she understood — in the way that only someone waiting for their own death can understand — that time was not infinite.

She started spending afternoons in the sick houses.

At first, no one noticed. There were always people coming and going from the places where plague survivors, aging fishermen, and the chronically ill crowded together. [[Mira]], however, began to stay.

She would sit with someone and listen to their breathing. She would count the shallow rises and falls of their chests. She would watch the light in their eyes and, without being told, understand when the end was approaching.

She would not leave before that end came.

By the time [[Mira]] had turned 20, [[Kael]] understood what [[Mira]] was doing before she fully understood it herself.

He recognized it because he had done something similar when his wife was dying. He had sat with her through her final days and understood, with a sort of cruel clarity, that the only thing he could give her was the certainty that when she left, someone would know she had existed.

"You don't have to do this," he told [[Mira]] once, watching her prepare to leave for another evening in the sick houses.

"I know," [[Mira]] replied. "But if I don't, they die alone."

"They're already alone," [[Kael]] said gently. "Death is the ultimate solitude. You can't change that."

[[Mira]] turned to face him. She was still young, but there was something ancient in her eyes — something that had learned too much about loss already.

"No," she said. "But I can change whether it's invisible alone. I can change whether their passing is truly solitary, and if someone has memories of their life."

[[Kael]] looked at his adoptive daughter — this girl he had raised from abandonment, this girl who was slowly becoming luminous with renewed purpose — and he understood what he was seeing: [[Mira]] was not the child she once was, even the nicknames felt awkward now. He was, instead, watching someone figure out how to make peace with the fact that they are dying.

He said nothing more.

He held her hand and let her go.

The Second Wave of the [[Great Plague]] had truly ended while [[Mira]] was still a child, way before [[Mira]] began her work, but it left scars that never truly healed.

The [[Great Plague]] had erased so many families. The song of many bloodlines fell silent. And [[Mira]] learned from the stories of the weeping ill that those who survived had done so partially through luck and partially through the deliberate choice to isolate.

It was hard to be away from others, but the most brutal truth wasn't about minimizing contact but about accepting that loving people in plague times meant watching them die. Some of the survivors had developed a theology about this and the glowing lights in the sky that shine when the night is at its darkest.

They called themselves the devout of the [[Auroral Ribbons]]. Their doctrine was simple: the [[Moon]] that hung above [[Lune Shallow]] was weeping. Something understood loss so intimately that it was trying to send comfort through the only channel available: the [[Lunehymn]], the silvery liquid that flowed from the [[Leylines]].

These pilgrims began collecting [[Lunehymn]], but they weren't carrying it for healing; instead, it was for them a sacred vial in revelation. When the liquid was most concentrated, it shifted from its regular pale silvery shine into a deep, midnight blue, with slight sparkles that mirrored the stars of the cosmos.

In a sense, the liquid was a gaze into the sky, even if it seemed bound to the soil, yet undeniably reflecting the heavens. Its complexity was truly mesmerizing.

They would drink it and fall into dreams so vivid and directed that it was almost like receiving visits from a [[Consciousness]] so large and so sad that it could only communicate through the language of dreams.

In these dreams, the devout began to understand something: whatever it was in the [[Moon]] was not looking for worship. It was looking for understanding. It was almost as if it was trying to explain what it is to be frail, imprisoned, but essential to the untouched. Even in their own fragility, they still choose to pour love into a world that could not return it. It was **"A love so pure it doesn't require love."**

The pilgrims not only saw the [[Auroral Ribbons]]. They also watched [[Mira]].

They saw a girl who had been left behind as a child, raised by someone else's mercy, slowly dying from the frailty of their condition, yet even in her weakness, she chose to spend her evenings comforting the endings of others that could not prevent their own death.

And they recognized that [[Mira]] was already doing what the [[Moon]] had been trying to do. [[Mira]] was the living answer to the [[Moon]] weeping dreams.

However, not everything would always be so beautiful.

Two years went by, and finally the devastating yet silent Third Wave of the [[Great Plague]] came. It did not announce itself until it had already begun.

A fisherman coughs at the market. A child develops a fever. A wife wakes to find her husband struggling for breath. Within days, even the carefully maintained isolation that [[Lune Shallow]] had relied on for safety since the start of [[Great Plague]] shatters.

The [[Great Plague]] arrives with the spring tides, carried perhaps by traders from outside, or by the simple inevitability of disease finding every hiding place eventually after one too many outsider caravans have arrived.

[[Kael]] is not young. He is 57 years old, and decades of work on the water had weathered his body. His lungs are already compromised and strained from constant exposure to salt air and harsh labor.

He knows, when he first begins to cough, precisely what is happening.

He does not tell [[Mira]] immediately.

Instead, he continues to rise at dawn. He continues to prepare to go to the boats. He does all the small rituals of normalcy for three days before [[Mira]] realizes. One morning, she finds him collapsed in the kitchen, coughing blood onto the floor. And the conversation that follows is the most important conversation of her life.

[[Mira]] kneels beside her father and does not weep. She has learned that weeping accomplishes nothing.

Instead, she asks: "How long have you known?"

[[Kael]] looks up at his daughter, who is now tending to him instead of him tending to her. He sees in [[Mira]] the woman who has grown from an abandoned child into someone wise and kind, and he tells her the truth.

"Since the first cough. I've lived long enough to recognize my own ending." [[Kael]] tries to make eye contact with her but he ultimately can't, "It has taken years for anything to take a toll on you, [[Mira]]. But I won't be here for the next [[Cycle]]."

[[Mira]] helps him to bed. She brings him water. She sits beside him and does the thing she has learned to do: she stays with him as he passes, slow yet sure.

"I'm sorry, my daughter," [[Kael]] says after a long silence with the first tears that [[Mira]] has ever seen in him. "I'm sorry I have to leave you again. I know what abandonment is like. I know what it does to you and in the end I couldn't fully make peace with it either."

[[Mira]] takes his hand. Her grip is steady, even though her body is betraying her too, even though she knows she will not be far behind him.

"You didn't abandon me the first time, Father," she says. "You saved me. And you're not abandoning me now. You're dying. There's a difference."

"Is there, Sweet tooth?" [[Kael]] asks, with a limp smile and genuine uncertainty in his voice, now whispering the final time [[Mira]] will hear that name. "From where you're standing, does it feel different?"

[[Mira]] considers this with absolute honesty.

"No," she finally says. "It feels like losing everything. But at least this time, I understand that it has to happen. Before, I didn't even know why or what was being taken away from me."

**[[Ballad]] Fragment IV. [[Kael]]**

[[Kael]]'s breathing becomes more labored as the days pass.

He declines rapidly — faster than the typical progression, as if his body is in a hurry to leave. Within a week, he is barely conscious. Within ten days, his breathing is shallow and irregular.

[[Mira]] sits with him constantly.

She barely sleeps. She does not leave home. But she does what she has learned to do with everyone else: she witnesses [[Kael]]’s final moments, tending to his care.

But this time, it is different.

This time, she is not a stranger offering presence to someone she has just met. This time, she is a daughter holding the hand of the man who chose to raise her, who decided to love her despite knowing it would end exactly this way.

Then her dreaded night finally arrives: a night when the moon is dark—a new moon, a phase when the [[Lunehymn]] does not flow, when the [[Leylines]] are quieter, when [[Arcanoria]] itself seems to hold its breath.

[[Kael]]'s breathing becomes something else entirely.

It becomes the breathing of someone whose lungs have filled with despair, whose body is drowning in its own failure.

[[Mira]] holds his hand and counts the moments between gasps.

She watches the light in his eyes begin to dim.

And when the moment comes — that precise, countable moment where he stops being someone struggling to breathe and becomes someone who has stopped breathing — [[Mira]] is present.

She sees it. She is the one witness clinging to his deathbed. She is the last in this world to register that [[Kael]] exists, before his existence becomes her memory.

And then she is alone in the house they have shared for over 2 decades, and the weight of that loneliness pierces her heart in a pain that her own sickness could never even compare.

It is not the aloneness of a child whose father had abandoned them. It is the aloneness of someone who has loved someone and watched them depart, and now must choose what to do with the absence they leave behind.

For two days after [[Kael]]'s death, [[Mira]] holds still. She is still clinging to him. In the exact position of her clenched heart, she does not eat or sleep.

She sits in the house and feels the weight of every ending she has ever witnessed, compressed now into her own body, her own loss.

She understands, for the first time, that witnessing the deaths of strangers was practice. It was preparation. But nothing — nothing — prepares you for seeing someone you love.

She understands that this is a wound that will not close. That she will carry [[Kael]]'s absence for the rest of her life, even if that too is increasingly limited.

On the third day — still without sleep — [[Mira]]'s body finally passes out from exhaustion.

She dreams of her father, desperately running, yet composed in singing her a lullaby. She never forgot the melody, even if fog deeply clouded the memory. The sweetness of it made her solitude bearable, even if the only truth she knew of her home was the harmony of it.

When she woke up, she was curled on the floor. She had a burning feeling in her eyes from crying in her sleep, but her hands were clenching a small, teardrop gem, appearing as if it had always been there, waiting for her to break open enough to find it.

It was pulsing with her heartbeat in a beautiful midnight purple, fading through a fine veinwork of black branches. She just had her [[Motif Awakening]] to [[Void]], the element of absence itself, in the dark hues of the space that is no longer there.

She does not understand what has happened — that the intensity of her grief has crystallized her [[Consciousness]] into the one binding that could hold it: the power to thread emptiness as deeply as presence.

She carefully holds the gem in her trembling hands and understands one thing: the absence is absolute now. And this gem, her [[Soul Leitmotif]] humming with the sweet lullaby of her bygone memory, is proof that [[Kael]] existed, that her orphaned family existed, because something in [[Mira]] broke when they all left her behind.

She sits on the floor with the gem in her palms and rocks back and forth, not weeping now, but in a state beyond weeping. In shock. In sleeplessness. In a hunger so profound it has stopped hurting and become a kind of hollow feeling.

She fidgets with the gem endlessly, her fingers tracing its curves, feeling its warmth— the pulsing of her own heartbeat, crystallized, made tangible.

"This is proof," she whispers to no one, to everyone, to the absence itself. "This is proof I loved. This is proof that they were all real."

Later that day, once a full [[Moon]] is clear in the sky, there is a knock on the door.

It is [[Selah]], the leader of the pilgrims following the [[Auroral Ribbons]].

[[Selah]] enters through the unlocked door and sees immediately that [[Mira]] is destroyed. She is breaking. She has barely slept, not eaten, and she is clutching something that glows faintly in the shadows of her clenched hand  —her newly awakened [[Soul Leitmotif]], her grief made [[Crystal]].

[[Mira]]'s eyes are hollow. Her skin has taken on a translucent quality. She looks like someone who is already halfway between the world and whatever comes after.

[[Selah]] kneels beside her and does something unexpected: she does not offer comfort or solutions. Instead, she reaches out and gently opens [[Mira]]'s clenched fist.

The [[Void]] gem rests there, pulsing softly.

[[Selah]] understands what she is seeing immediately. "You've awakened," [[Selah]] says, and filled her voice with something like awe. "You've awakened a [[Void]] binding. That means—"

"It means he's gone," [[Mira]] interrupts, her voice paper-thin. "It means they are all gone, and that absence is real. It means I'm proof that he existed because something in me broke when he left."

[[Selah]] sits with her. She sits in the destruction and says, "He was good. And he's gone. And you loved him. And that doesn't make it better."

For the first time in her life, [[Mira]] truly breaks. She lets herself cry in all of her profound feelings. [[Selah]] embraces her.

For hours, she cries while [[Selah]] tends to her decaying body. She cries for the father she never met, for the fisherman who raised her, for every person she's ever sat with in their final moments, for herself, and the days she has left.

And as she cries, something else happens.

The [[Auroral Ribbons]] begin to shimmer in the window with the light of the people who had passed that night. Not faintly, as they usually do. But visibly, actively, almost as if responding to her grief with their own kind of luminescence.

[[Selah]] prays to them. And as she does, she sees a vision on their reflection. One single star of the vast, immense sky reflecting the golden light of the ribbons. For [[Selah]] this is the signal that it is [[Mira]]'s grief the light of that same star in her darkest night. For [[Selah]], [[Mira]] truly is the chosen of the [[Moon]].

When [[Mira]]'s weeping finally subdues, [[Selah]] speaks.

"We've been watching you. For two years, we've been watching you sit with the dying and offer presence. And we've been understanding something. The [[Lunehymn]] that flows here—it's not just a healing agent. It's a form of communication. Something in the [[Moon]] is trying to reach us. And every time you sit with someone while they die, every time you witness an ending, you're answering that call."

[[Mira]] looks at her with broken, flooded eyes, utterly human in their vulnerability.

"What are you asking?" [[Mira]] says, though she begins to suspect.

Sera takes a long breath. "There's something vast watching you. Something lonely. And I think it's grieving too—for something or someone we can't see. The [[Auroral Ribbons]] shimmer brighter when you're near the dying. It's like the [[Moon]] itself is trying to speak through you."

She pauses carefully.

"We want to ask if you would be willing to transform that grief into something larger. If you would be willing to let what you're carrying right now—this awakening, this presence, this understanding of what it means to witness absence—become something that reaches everyone."

[[Mira]] looks down at the [[Void]] gem in her hand.

"How?" she asks.

"We don't know," [[Selah]] admits while looking out the window. "We've never done this. But we believe that if we create the right conditions—if we gather people who understand grief, who understand presence—then the thing watching from the [[Moon]] might step forward. And if you were willing to meet it..."

[[Selah]] trails off, letting the implication sit.

**[[Ballad]] Fragment V. [[Lacrimosa]]**

[[Mira]] reaches out and takes what appears to be [[Lacrimosa]]'s hand—the ghost of a hand, the approximation of touch that an [[Outer God]] and a dying girl can manage. Her lungs were burning with effort, her body already beginning the severe decline into the final weeks of her illness.

For [[Mira]], it is confirmation that what she is experiencing is not madness, but something as fundamental as death, as grief, as loss.

[[Mira]] begins singing to the moon-swept sea below, the melody of her [[Soul Leitmotif]] as her lullaby, as the omen to the melody of the [[Moon]].

**[[Ballad]] Fragment VI. The Twin [[Moon]]s**

While the ritual ends, over the course of the three full [[Moon]]s that mark [[Mira]]'s final months of life, they speak.

Not constantly. [[Mira]] does not have the energy for that. But on the nights when the [[Moon]] is full, when the [[Lunehymn]] flows strongest, they meet in the sanctuary and talk.

Two months after [[Kael]]'s death, [[Lacrimosa]] begins to understand what presence and passing meant.

[[Mira]] tells her about every person she has ever sat with while they died.

[[Mira]] carefully thinks of her following words. "I believe this is a beautiful way to comfort their despair, but... I'm not really thinking that, I just wish I could have given them peace before the pain found anyone."

[[Mira]] then sighs with relief.

"Have you thought about it?" [[Mira]] asks, her voice brittle now, each word deliberate and counted.

[[Lacrimosa]] looks at her, and there is something wounded in her gaze.

[[Mira]] is first contemplative in silence, but then she reassures her. "I know, I will die regardless, and I've known since three years, and I've been trying to make peace with it since I began witnessing the passing of others, but this fear is not something that witnessing washes away." She suddenly stops to gather courage. "I— want to transcend at least... if I have the chance to make my death mean something."

"Tell me what it is that frightens you most, please!" [[Mira]] says in a resonant, powerful voice for the first time.

[[Lacrimosa]], startled, is silent for a long time before speaking.

"Erasure— And the piercing clarity to realize all that would cease wrong. That if I step into the world as you're asking, I will no longer be separate. She pauses, and when she continues, her voice is barely audible:

[[Mira]]'s thumb traces the back of [[Lacrimosa]]'s hand—or tries to, though her touch passes through something formless.

"I wasn't always orphaned," [[Mira]] begins, and [[Lacrimosa]] understands: this is the confession she has been waiting for. "My biological father was dying, and he brought me to a safer place. [[Lacrimosa]]'s form becomes almost translucent, beginning to fracture with emotion that mirrors the tears running through the cheeks of the soft, ill-touched edges of [[Mira]]'s face.

[[Lacrimosa]] closes her hollowed eyes. But she is not thinking about [[Mira]]'s lesson. She is thinking about something else. Something that sounds similar but is rooted in something different.

Her form trembles, and after a pause, she speaks.

[[Mira]]'s eyes widen slightly.

"Then you understand," [[Mira]] says gently. "You understand what it means to lose someone without ever having had them. To miss someone who was never yours to have."

[[Lacrimosa]] nods, unable to speak.

"I'm afraid," [[Lacrimosa]] admits.

"I know," [[Mira]] whispers. "So am I. But we can be afraid together. That's what witnessing the last moments means."

After a silence, [[Mira]] stands pointing to the skies. "Maybe that is the [[Purest of Love]]. A love so pure it maybe doesn't require love," she briefly pauses. "Maybe... it could be, too, something, almost like intimacy... what you can do for me, when I finally rest." [[Mira]] says softly, in pained words, barely able to speak through her plea. "I could be— finally? An... an architect of something?" [[Lacrimosa]] replies in the fractured voice of a lost fantasy.

And now, looking at the [[Moon]], [[Mira]] hums that sweet melody that reminds her of a gentler past.

[[Lacrimosa]], in silence, retreats. She is still processing what [[Mira]] just said. And the thought of action drives her impossibly mad to everything that could fail.

The dream suddenly ends, but [[Lacrimosa]] learns that presence is not about saving anyone. It is about bearing witness to the fact that they existed, and that their suffering isn't only meaningful but rather the freedom that the release of suffering gives.

She learns that the girl she has been speaking to—this ordinary, orphaned, dying girl—understands something that she, herself, has spent eons trying to grasp in [[The Infinite Void]]: that invisibility is only unbearable if you stop trying to reach toward others. That loneliness only becomes absolute if you stop being present to it. It is the merger of two [[Consciousness]], which makes their suffering into [[Consonance]].

**[[Ballad]] Fragment VII. [[Mira]]**

Six months after [[Kael]]'s death. The final full [[Moon]] rises, the last one [[Mira]] will see.

She is skeletal now, nearly as translucent as [[Lacrimosa]]. Her breathing is a conscious effort. Her voice has become something thin and reedy, like a wind instrument at the edge of breaking.

[[Lacrimosa]] grips [[Mira]]'s hand—or tries to, though her form is beginning to waver as the night deepens.

"I don't understand death," [[Lacrimosa]] says, and it is a confession born from genuine fear. "I have observed it countless times, but I don't understand it. I don't understand how someone stops being."

"It hurts, but life and every end in itself does, because that's the [[Weight of Change]]." [[Mira]] confirms. "But only the ending of their life is final. She pauses.

"And if you witness for them after I'm gone—if you reach out to those who are grieving, those who are in pain—then I too will continue through your presence, even if I'm not here. Everyone I ever loved will continue through the work you do."

[[Lacrimosa]]'s form fractures further, beginning to become almost transparent with emotion. Unable to maintain a solid link.

"I don't know how to let you go," [[Lacrimosa]] says.

The dual [[Moon]] is full, as above them as it is below in the windswept ocean across the cliff. The [[Lunehymn]] river flows thickly through the [[Leylines]], almost as if responding to the intensity of this moment. A clear, beautiful sky, reflecting the landscape of the lullaby [[Mira]] always sang.

As the night deepens, [[Mira]]'s breathing becomes fainter.

Then fainter.

Then it becomes something else, barely clinging.

[[Lacrimosa]] sits beside her, holding her hand, embracing her, and she experiences something she has never experienced in her entire existence: she is present for something ending, and she is choosing not to retreat.

She is choosing to bear witness.

[[Mira]]'s eyes, which have been dimming for hours, suddenly focus one last time.

"I can see it," Mira whispers. "The light. Not in the sky, but in you. Your [[Auroral Ribbons]] are beautiful. I feel scared, but they are comforting. Her [[Void]] [[Soul Leitmotif]] now flickers, not just with her heartbeat, but as if the glow itself is dimming out. The soft purple receding to black.

In one last effort, [[Mira]] points to her ribbon, to her brooch, to her heart.

"Don't go," [[Lacrimosa]] says, and it is the first true prayer she has ever spoken, "I'm not ready to be invisible again."

[[Mira]]'s gentle smile becomes beatific, even as her eyes begin to glaze.

"You are here," she whispers. "You've been learning your whole existence. You just have to choose to act."

Where [[Mira]]'s hand finally goes still.

Where one [[Consciousness]] dissolves, and another learns what it means to remain.

She does not shatter.
